A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: V3 reports original experiments on six multi-agent systems across four tasks, including error-injection analyses and evaluations of Challenger and Inspector.

after.justification: V4 retains original empirical results and adds experiments involving faulty single agents, simultaneous faults, graph variants, additional models, and software construction.

M1.justification: AutoTransform, AutoInject, Challenger, and Inspector retain their procedures and prompts. Appendix C is unchanged. The additional graph configurations extend evaluation rather than revise these proposed methods.

E1.justification: The four benchmark datasets remain unchanged. Appendix B.5 adds complete Snake-game construction in pygame, extending evaluation beyond isolated programming functions. Appendix B.3 also introduces scenarios with simultaneous faulty agents.

E2.justification: The six principal systems and defense comparisons remain. Appendix B.2 adds compromised single-agent comparators to the faulty-system comparison. B.4 evaluates four-agent complete and star graphs inspired by GPTSwarm and MacNet; these are described as implementations inspired by those frameworks, not evaluations of their full published methods.

E3.justification: The main benchmark settings are retained, but new experiments substantially extend the evaluation design: requested 20%/40% AutoTransform error rates, paired faulty roles in AgentVerse, matched four-agent graph configurations, LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct tests, and o1-Mini math evaluation. These are additional configurations, not evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds analyses of AutoTransform's error-rate fidelity, simultaneous faults involving planners versus critics, transfer to complete/star graphs, and resilience with additional backbones. It also adds the Snake-game case study. The existing error-category analysis, error-rate/type experiments, and HumanEval cases are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix B.1 newly reports standard deviations and minimum/maximum realized error rates for AutoTransform's 20% and 40% targets. V3 provides no corresponding variability estimates. Neither version supplies benchmark confidence intervals or explicit repeated-run/seed counts.

E6.justification: The task table changes substantially: for example, GPT-4o AutoTransform code performance changes from 73.78 in v3 Table 6 to 58.49 in v4 Table 5. These are tabulated reporting revisions; Figure 4's plotted data are retained. Appendix B.2–B.6 adds numerous numerical and qualitative findings. Structure-level raw scores, error-rate/type tables, and defense Table 3 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 2 adds formal graph definitions and degree constraints for the three structures, including a rooted, acyclic tree definition of hierarchy. V3 provides informal communication patterns only. The new hierarchy constraint conflicts with the retained bidirectional hierarchical example; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain, but the abstract revises headline drops from 9.2%/26.0%/31.2% to 5.5%/10.5%/23.7%. The former match relative GPT-3.5 AutoInject losses; the latter match averaged score losses from retained structure results. The abstract also describes 96.4% recovery as errors recovered, while Section 5 still measures recovery of lost performance.

C2.justification: Appendix D replaces the assertion that no additional influencing factors were found with explicit prompt/implementation confounding and limits on extrapolation beyond the studied tasks. RQ1 changes its explanation of linear-system weakness from lacking leadership to slow communication and limited oversight. New appendices interpret planner-driven failure propagation and generalization across models and graph structures.

D1.justification: V4 newly specifies direct messaging without summarization or broadcasting, and documents additional model identifiers, four-agent graph arrangements, and pygame usage. These additions improve documentation without establishing changes to the retained main experiments. Existing prompt templates and the code/data access URL are unchanged.

R1.justification: V4 adds agent-reliability and topology literature, including NetSafe, AgentSafe, G-Safeguard, and CORBA. Section 6.2 newly distinguishes NetSafe through subjective-task coverage and code-error analysis. Most existing related-work discussion and contribution positioning remain intact.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory passages, structural interpretation, and limitations receive localized rewrites. Experimental Settings becomes unnumbered, quantitative results move from Appendix B to A, and error analysis becomes B.1. The ethics statement moves into the main text as Impact Statement; its substance is retained.

P2.justification: Figure 4 changes from side-by-side panels to vertically stacked panels, while existing schematics receive visual refinements. Quantitative tables gain average rows/columns and explicit single-agent rows, and Tables 9–10 are added. The general document layout and existing figure content remain recognizable.

improvement.justification: V4 brings the task table into better agreement with retained Figure 4, adds relevant robustness evidence, and acknowledges prompt/implementation confounding. However, its new tree definition conflicts with its bidirectional hierarchy, Table 9 reports an AutoTransform average of 21.66 although its listed scores average 24.77, and Appendix D still claims GPT-only experiments despite B.6. These new inconsistencies affect interpretation and the reliability of the added evidence, leaving the net quality direction uncertain.
